synopsis: Distributional agreement compares the spreads of repeated simulated and measured results, rather than matching individual runs or points, because perception trials and sensor returns legitimately vary [f14749, f14750, f4801, f12621, f7802]. The booklet recommends multi-level, multi-metric validation, including distributions and downstream perception or closed-loop outcomes; sensor-family reports should use withheld real raw data rather than rely on visual realism [f14716, f14797, f10558]. In a November 2025 on-road study, density-aware Chamfer distance correlated best with perception among the metrics compared, but real-versus-simulated scans averaged DCD 0.63 with only 21% segmentation mIoU, and prediction of safety-relevant perception errors remains uncertain [f4815, f4816, f5067]. The area validation metric measures the area between simulated and measured cumulative distributions in the output quantity’s units; the booklet treats it as model-form uncertainty and describes extrapolating it to untested conditions as an additional prediction margin [f7796, f7797, f7798]. Its acceptance role is disputed because greater experimental scatter can make a model appear better, and mixing epistemic and aleatory uncertainty can produce over- or under-compensation [f7799, f7800, f8191]. Rail validation supplies an established distribution-based analogue, using at least 24 comparisons per quantity across at least 12 track sections, with statistics and limits applied to the deviations [f7803, f7804, f7805, f7807].
